17.1 Alkyl Halides

Halogen derivatives of alkanes are called haloalkanes. Haloalkanes are formed by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms from alkanes by halogens. They are also called organohalogen compounds. Haloalkanes may be monohaloalkanes, dihaloalkanes, trihaloalkanes etc., depending upon the number of halogen atoms present in the molecule.

They are represented by R–X, where R- is an alkyl group represented by CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ and –X is halogen which is the functional group. The general formula of alkyl halides is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X, where n represents the number of carbon atoms.

Alkyl halides are classified according to the nature of the carbon atom bonded to the halogen. If the halogen-bearing carbon is bonded to one carbon atom, it is primary (1°) and the alkyl halide is a primary alkyl halide. If two carbon atoms are bonded to the halogen-bearing carbon, it is secondary (2°) and the compound is a secondary alkyl halide. A tertiary alkyl halide (3°) has three other carbon atoms bonded to the halogen–bearing carbon atom. If the halogen-bearing carbon atom is a methyl group (bonded to no other carbon atoms), the compound is a methyl halide.

Unit 17 — Alkyl Halides and Amines

After studying this unit, students will be able to:

Name alkyl halides using IUPAC system. (Applying)

Discuss the structure and reactivity of RX. (Applying)

Introduction

17.1 Alkyl Halides

Halogen derivatives of alkanes are called haloalkanes. Haloalkanes are formed by replacing one or more hydrogen atoms from alkanes by halogens. They are also called organohalogen compounds. Haloalkanes may be monohaloalkanes, dihaloalkanes, trihaloalkanes etc., depending upon the number of halogen atoms present in the molecule.

Monohaloalkanes are usually called alkyl halides. The functional group of alkyl halides is halogen. They are represented by R–X, where R- is an alkyl group represented by CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ and –X is halogen which is the functional group. The general formula of alkyl halides is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X, where n represents the number of carbon atoms.

Alkyl halides are classified according to the nature of the carbon atom bonded to the halogen. If the halogen-bearing carbon is bonded to one carbon atom, it is primary (1°) and the alkyl halide is a primary alkyl halide. If two carbon atoms are bonded to the halogen-bearing carbon, it is secondary (2°) and the compound is a secondary alkyl halide. A tertiary alkyl halide (3°) has three other carbon atoms bonded to the halogen–bearing carbon atom. If the halogen-bearing carbon atom is a methyl group (bonded to no other carbon atoms), the compound is a methyl halide.

17.1.1 Nomenclature

There are two ways of naming alkyl halides. The common (trivial) system and systematic (IUPAC) nomenclature.
